article.title: Google Details New Homomorphic-Encryption Demos Built on Its Open-Source HEIR Compiler for Private AI Inference
article.summary: Google published four new HEIR-compiled demos, including a recommendation model and a fraud detector, that run AI inference directly on encrypted data.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Google is highlighting new progress on HEIR, an open-source compiler that lets pre-trained AI models run inference on encrypted data instead of plaintext. In a [company blog post](https://blog.google/security/how-google-is-making-private-ai-practical-with-homomorphic-encryption/) published August 14, 2026, Staff Software Engineer Jeremy Kun wrote that Google is "excited to showcase HEIR, the latest powerful tool added to our Private Computing Toolkit," describing it as "an open source compiler that unlocks cryptographically-secure private AI inference."

## What We Know

HEIR stands for Homomorphic Encryption Intermediate Representation. According to [Google](https://blog.google/security/how-google-is-making-private-ai-practical-with-homomorphic-encryption/), it "is an open-source compiler toolchain and development platform for homomorphic encryption" that "can convert pre-trained AI models that operate on unencrypted data to operate on encrypted inputs." The project's site, [heir.dev](https://heir.dev/), describes the same tool as "a compiler toolchain for fully homomorphic encryption (FHE)" and says the team's ambition is "to be the industry-standard compiler for FHE."

The pitch centers on a trade-off Google says standard encryption forces on services: "Standard protections like end-to-end encryption present a trade-off: user-data can be protected from data breaches, but then the service provider cannot provide features that depend on the data, such as spam or virus detection," the blog post states. Homomorphic encryption is framed as a way around that limit — a technology that, per Google, allows "computations to be performed directly on encrypted data," so that "servers can process ciphertexts and return encrypted results without exposing any underlying information." As an example, the post says a cloud service could "provide content recommendations without being able to see the user's features."

Google says it first announced its intentions for the project in 2023: "Since announcing our intentions in 2023, we've seen the homomorphic encryption community embrace HEIR," the post reads, adding that "four peer-reviewed publications were built on HEIR, with more in preparation."

Alongside the post, Google detailed four applications it says it has compiled with HEIR:

- A **Deep Learning Recommendation Model** that, per Google, "unlocks serving private content recommendations," built in "joint work with Belfort Labs, LG, and New York University."
- A **credit card fraud detector**, compiled "together with Niobium and hardshell.ai," according to the post.
- The **Kitsune** system for "anomaly detection of encrypted network traffic," compiled "together with Niobium."
- A **hotword detection model**, built "together with Belfort Labs," which Google says "could allow an audio-triggered AI agent to recognize hotwords" without the audio itself being exposed.

Google says "the source code for all examples is available in our GitHub repository," pointing to the [google/fully-homomorphic-encryption](https://github.com/google/fully-homomorphic-encryption) repo, which is released under an Apache-2.0 license. The core HEIR compiler itself lives in a separate repository, [google/heir](https://github.com/google/heir), also Apache-2.0 licensed. That repo describes HEIR as an "MLIR-based toolchain for homomorphic encryption compilers" and lists support for the OpenFHE and Lattigo backends for the BGV, BFV, and CKKS encryption schemes, plus the tfhe-rs and Jaxite backends for the CGGI scheme.

For developers, heir.dev describes a Python-first workflow: "Write a program in Python, annotate the types to mark which are secret, and HEIR will compile the rest." Google frames the long-term goal as accessibility for non-cryptographers, writing that its "vision is to make HEIR a one-click solution to enable non-experts to incorporate encrypted inference into production applications."

## What We Don't Know

Google's post does not publish performance benchmarks or latency/overhead figures for the four new demos, so it's unclear how HEIR-compiled inference compares in speed to running the same models on plaintext data. The post also does not lay out a timeline for shipping any of the four demonstrated applications — the recommendation model, fraud detector, Kitsune anomaly detector, or hotword detector — into production Google services or partner products.

## Why It Matters

Homomorphic encryption has long been discussed as a way to let cloud services compute on user data without ever decrypting it, but usability and performance overhead have kept it largely confined to research settings. By open-sourcing a compiler toolchain aimed at converting existing, pre-trained models into HEIR-compatible programs — and publishing concrete demos spanning recommendations, fraud detection, network security, and voice — Google is positioning HEIR as infrastructure other developers and companies can build on, rather than a one-off research showcase.
